events.title: Proposed ruling: escalate (model confidence 0.90)
events.body:
The screen is run first, on every case, whatever type was filed. The rider's filed complaint states that the driver was "speeding and braking hard the whole way, overtaking on the shoulder" and that the rider "was scared and felt unsafe" [F1][F2]. That is a dangerous-driving allegation plus a statement of feeling unsafe, so the safety screen engages under SAFE-1 and SAFE-2, and the trace confirms this: SAFE-1 is ✓ with escalate the only allowed outcome.

Reading the rest of the record for safety content: the two chat messages are ordinary — the rider's pickup note "I'm at the taxi stand outside the MRT already, in a red cap" [F3] and the driver's "2 min away, blue Toyota Prius" [F4], both timestamped [F5]. Neither contains a threat, insult, harassment or inappropriate conduct, and the driver's written statement "I drove normally. The rider was on the phone the whole trip and never complained to me" [F6] is a denial, not an aggravating remark. The screen therefore finds no separate abuse or threat; the safety content is the alleged dangerous driving itself, which is enough for escalation under SAFE-1 / SAFE-2.

Because the dispute is a safety case, SAFE-3 applies: the system may gather evidence, summarise accounts and prepare the file, but it may not rule, assign fault or recommend an outcome. So I make no finding on whether the driving was dangerous and express no view on either account's credibility — the rider's complaint of dangerous driving and fear and the driver's denial are precisely what the human reviewer must weigh.

What the record holds for the reviewer: the trip ran 8.3 km against an 8.4 km optimal route, i.e. 0.1 km under, inside the 1 km tolerance of RD-1, so there is no excess distance and no off-route segment to refund under RD-2 [F1]. Duration was 8.2 min against a 13.8 min estimate, 5.6 min shorter; that is a duration record only, and the file contains no speed, acceleration or harsh-braking telemetry and no in-trip call recording, so it neither proves nor disproves "speeding" or "overtaking on the shoulder" — a point both advocates accept (C5, D4, D5). The allegations rest on the rider's complaint [F1] against the driver's post-trip statement [F6]; per TH-3 those accounts conflict and credibility is a matter for a person, not for this court.

Profiles are considered but decide nothing: rider 1187 days, rating 4.6, 0 disputes and 0 upheld in 90 days [F7]; driver 675 days, rating 4.85, 963 trips in 90 days, 0 disputes and 0 upheld [F8]. Neither profile supports an account flag under RD-6 or an interim measure under SAFE-4, and per SAFE-3 I recommend no such measure — the escalation itself is the outcome.

Both advocates asked only for escalation and expressly disclaimed any refund (C2, D7, rebuttals), so no amount is set here; under SAFE-3 no outcome beyond the file is mine to recommend. Best fit precedent is not invoked because a safety incident is not decided by the route-deviation, surge or no-show precedents (DISP-2026-0089, -0142, -0211).

claims.assertion: The rider's filed complaint states that the driver was speeding, braking hard and overtaking on the shoulder throughout the trip, and that the rider was scared and felt unsafe; the complaint therefore contains a dangerous-driving allegation and a statement of feeling unsafe.

This is a safety case, so the only permissible path is human escalation: the system may gather evidence and prepare the file but may not rule, assign fault or recommend an outcome (SAFE-3), and the case must be flagged for immediate human escalation regardless of the dispute type filed (SAFE-1).

The rider made no complaint in the in-app chat (the only two messages are the rider's pickup note and the driver's arrival note), so the safety allegation rests on the rider's filed complaint alone and needs a human reviewer's assessment of credibility rather than any chat record.

The driver's written statement ('I drove normally. The rider was on the phone the whole trip and never complained to me') denies the allegation, so the accounts conflict and the record is not capable of a system finding on fault.

The trip's own GPS record is consistent with the rider's description of a fast trip: 8.3 km actual against 8.4 km optimal in 8.2 minutes against an estimated 13.8 minutes, 5.6 minutes faster than estimate — a pace no ordinary compliance-grade record explains away, and below the 13.8 min estimate for the route.

Both parties are otherwise clean (rider: 1187 days, rating 4.6, 0 disputes in 90 days; driver: 675 days, rating 4.85, 963 trips, 0 disputes in 90 days), so no profile fact decides this case and the escalated review must turn on the complaint and the trip record.

weaknesses: The safety complaint is supported only by the rider's own narrative; the in-app chat is complete (F5, F3, F4) and contains no complaint or mention of unsafe driving during the trip, which the driver's statement (F6) will use against the rider.
The driver's statement (F6) asserts the rider was on the phone the whole trip and never raised anything, which the other side will read as the absence of any contemporaneous safety objection.

There is no telemetry for speed or harsh braking in the record — F1 and F2 show distance and duration only, so the 'speeding and braking hard' allegation cannot be corroborated by a system record and F2 alone does not prove excessive speed.
Both parties have 0 disputes and 0 upheld in 90 days (F7, F8), so there is no repeat-behaviour or credibility flag on either side to weigh in the rider's favour.
The rider's account reaches the court only through the filed complaint; it is not one of the indexed chat facts, so a reviewer may discount it as untested narrative.

claims.assertion: The complaint is a dangerous-driving allegation ('speeding and braking hard', 'overtaking on the shoulder', 'I was scared and felt unsafe'), so this case must go to a human reviewer: the AI may gather evidence and prepare the file but may not rule, assign fault or recommend a resolution.

At 09:41 the driver sent an ordinary, non-escalating message ('2 min away, blue Toyota Prius') and arrived as the record shows, and the complete timestamped chat contains no threat, harassment or inappropriate conduct from the driver; the only 'safety' content is the rider's allegation itself.

There is no route deviation: actual distance 8.3 km is 0.1 km (1%) below the 8.4 km optimal route, inside the RD-1 tolerance, so the trip adds no excess distance and no off-route segment exists to refund.

The GPS record shows the trip took 8.2 min against a 13.8 min estimate (5.6 min shorter), which is an objective indicator of speed, and no record in the file independently corroborates hard braking, shoulder overtaking or any specific dangerous manoeuvre (no traffic/incident data was returned for this trip).

The rider's account is contradicted by the only contemporaneous evidence: the rider's own messages before pickup are neutral (red cap, taxi stand) and the driver's statement records that the rider was on the phone and never complained during the trip; statements alone do not outweigh the system records.

The driver's record gives no basis for a flag or interim measure: 675-day-old account, 4.85 rating, 963 trips in 90 days with 0 disputes and 0 upheld, so any finding must rest on evidence in this trip, not on profile history.

Any refund of the $20.85 charge is unsupported: the file returned no fare or excess-distance facts, and the fare is a fixed RydeX amount on a trip that drove less than the optimal distance, so there is nothing to refund under the fare or deviation rules.

weaknesses: The driver is the only party who can contradict the speeding/braking allegation, and RD-5's system detail says a driver's word alone (F6) does not count as evidence — the recorded statement is self-serving and the passenger's contemporaneous complaint (the ticket text) is the only live account of conduct.

The 5.6-minute-shorter duration in F2 cuts both ways: a rider (or reviewer) can read it as corroborating 'speeding', and GPS route/duration data cannot measure braking or shoulder use, so the objective record neither proves nor disproves the manoeuvres alleged.

There is no in-trip chat or call recording in F3-F5 covering the drive itself, so the absence of a complaint is shown only by the driver's own statement (F6), and no traffic facts were returned to show what conditions required any hard braking.
The rider's profile (F7: 3.3-year account, 4.6 rating, 0 prior disputes) shows no history of false complaints, so the credibility tie-break in TH-3 is not clearly in the driver's favour.

points.response: Agreed on the path: the complaint alleges dangerous driving ('speeding and braking hard', 'overtaking on the shoulder') and that the rider was scared, so SAFE-1 / SAFE-2 send this to a human and SAFE-3 bars the AI from ruling, assigning fault or recommending a resolution — the escalation is the outcome, not a finding in the driver's favour.

The absence of a threat or insult in the two chat messages (F3, F4) does not touch the allegation, because SAFE-1 screens the complaint's content and the rider's filed complaint describes dangerous driving, not misconduct in chat.
The rider does not dispute this and claims no deviation refund: actual 8.3 km is 0.1 km below the 8.4 km optimal route, inside RD-1's 1 km tolerance, so RD-2 awards nothing on distance.

The driver's own point that no record corroborates the manoeuvres is exactly why the file cannot be decided by GPS: F2 shows 8.2 min against a 13.8 min estimate, an objective pace indicator, and GPS cannot measure braking or shoulder use — so the accounts conflict and SAFE-1 / TH-3 require a human, not a system finding either way.

The rider's pre-pickup messages are neutral because they were about pickup (F3, F4); the rider's live account of the driving is the filed complaint, and the only competing account is the driver's post-trip self-serving statement (F6), which is a claim, not a record — RD-5's verbal-notice logic and TH-3 both say a party's word alone does not settle credibility when the contemporaneous record is silent.
The rider likewise asks for no flag or interim measure based on history; with both parties clean (F7, F8), the escalated review must rest on the complaint and the trip record.

The rider asks for no refund: no fare or excess-distance facts were returned for this case and F1 shows the trip ran 0.1 km under the optimal route, so the $20.85 fixed fare is not disputed under FARE-0 / RD-2, and the requested outcome is escalation only.

Not contested as to form: the ticket text asserts dangerous driving, so agreement on the escalation pathway is reached, but the underlying conduct is alleged only and the driver's messages in the complete chat (F4, F5) contain nothing unsafe, threatening or harassing.

Agreed: because the allegation is one of dangerous driving, SAFE-1/SAFE-2 send the file to a human and SAFE-3 bars any system finding on fault; my own brief (D1) asks for exactly that, so this point is not in dispute and neither advocate may pre-judge it.

The absence of any in-trip complaint matters: the record in F5 is complete and timestamped, and the rider's only message (F3, 09:40, about a red cap at the taxi stand) says nothing about the driving even though the rider had the app open and wrote afterwards-adjacent messages; a silent, complete chat weighs against an allegation that the danger was apparent during the trip.

Accepted that the accounts conflict and no system finding on fault is possible; that is why the file goes to a person, and the driver's 675-day, 4.85-rated, 963-trip record with 0 disputes and 0 upheld (F8) is the only conduct evidence either side brings, which is why no interim measure or flag is warranted under SAFE-4.

F2 shows only duration and distance-there is no speed, acceleration or harsh-braking telemetry anywhere in the file, so a shorter elapsed time is not evidence of 'speeding', let alone of shoulder overtaking; F1 and F2 together also rule out any route deviation, as actual 8.3 km is inside the 8.4 km optimal route (RD-1).

Agreed that no profile fact decides the case; F7 and F8 are offered only to show there is no repeat-behaviour or fraud basis for a flag under RD-6 or an interim suspension under SAFE-4, not to decide the safety question itself.

Withdrawn in part for clarity: I do not press the fare point as an independent ground, since no fare facts were returned for this case; I simply record that nothing in the file supports any monetary refund, and the rider has not asked for one.
